Avenge
uh-VENJ
v.
From Old French avengier, from Latin vindicare, to claim or lay legal claim to. Webster 1828: to vindicate; to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injurious person. In the Authorized Version the verb is almost always God’s, or the magistrate’s under God, and it is expressly forbidden to the private man.

Biblical Definition

The law forbids private vengeance in the same verse that commands neighbour-love: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD (Leviticus 19:18). David keeps it under maximum provocation: the LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee (1 Samuel 24:12) — he asks God for the vengeance and refuses to take it. God claims the act as His own: he will avenge the blood of his servants, and will render vengeance to his adversaries (Deuteronomy 32:43), and He executes it through appointed instruments — thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets (2 Kings 9:7). The New Testament repeats the prohibition and grounds it in the claim: Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord (Romans 12:19). Our Lord’s parable of the importunate widow makes crying for vengeance a form of persevering prayer (Luke 18:3-5), and the souls under the altar cry How long, O Lord… dost thou not judge and avenge our blood (Revelation 6:10). Believers are forbidden to take vengeance; they are not forbidden to ask for it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines AVENGE as to vindicate; to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injurious person; and notes that in Scripture the act belongs chiefly to God, who declares vengeance to be His own.

expand to see more

AVENGE, v.t. — To vindicate; to take satisfaction for an injury by punishing the injurious person; to revenge.

To take satisfaction for, by pain or punishment inflicted on the injuring party; as, to avenge blood.

AVENGER, n. — One who avenges or vindicates; a vindicator.

Webster’s vindicate is the better English word for the biblical idea. The point is not the discharge of anger but the setting right of a wrong, which is why the act belongs to a judge and not to the injured party.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 19:18 — "Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD."

1 Samuel 24:12 — "The LORD judge between me and thee, and the LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee."

2 Kings 9:7 — "And thou shalt smite the house of Ahab thy master, that I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets, and the blood of all the servants of the LORD, at the hand of Jezebel."

Romans 12:19 — "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."

Revelation 6:10 — "And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?"

Modern Corruption

The word is corrupted in two opposite ways: by the revenge culture that makes retaliation a virtue, and by the sentimental reading that treats God’s vengeance as beneath Him — which would leave the martyrs of Revelation 6:10 without an answer.

expand to see more

Romans 12:19 does not tell the believer that his injury does not matter. It tells him that the settling of it belongs to Someone else, and it quotes Deuteronomy 32 to prove it. The prohibition is therefore a comfort as well as a command: a Christian may hand over a wrong precisely because it will be dealt with, not because it will be forgotten. Where that confidence is lost, forgiveness curdles into denial or hardens into grievance. The next verse is remarkable for what it commands instead — if thine enemy hunger, feed him — which is possible only for a man who believes the account has been transferred and not cancelled.

The sentimental error runs the other way and cannot be squared with Revelation 6:10. The souls under the altar are martyrs, they are in heaven, and they cry out to a holy and true Lord asking how long until He avenges their blood. Their prayer is answered, not rebuked. A god who would never avenge would be a god indifferent to the murder of his own, and the moral universe would have no floor. Scripture holds both truths without strain: vengeance belongs to God, He will execute it, the civil magistrate bears the sword as His minister for the present (Romans 13:4), and the private believer keeps his hand off — as David did in the cave, with the man who was hunting him asleep within reach.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew root is naqam, to avenge or take vengeance; the Greek ekdikeo means to vindicate or execute justice out of a legal claim, and its noun is the New Testament word for vengeance.

expand to see more

Hebrew naqam (H5358) — to avenge, to take vengeance; forbidden to the private man in Leviticus 19:18, claimed by God in Deuteronomy 32:43.

Hebrew go'el ha-dam — the avenger of blood, the appointed kinsman whose office the cities of refuge regulate (Numbers 35).

Greek ekdikeo (G1556) — to vindicate, to avenge; the importunate widow’s plea (Luke 18:3) and the martyrs’ cry (Revelation 6:10).

Greek ekdikesis (G1557) — vengeance; Vengeance is mine; I will repay (Romans 12:19).

Greek ekdikos (G1558) — an avenger; the magistrate is God’s revenger to execute wrath (Romans 13:4).

Usage

"Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge (Leviticus 19:18) — the prohibition stands in the same verse as the command to love the neighbour."

"The LORD avenge me of thee: but mine hand shall not be upon thee (1 Samuel 24:12) — David asks for it and refuses to take it."

"Avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath (Romans 12:19) — the account is transferred, not cancelled."
